column4: The section contrasts day that shows itself with the day that “جَلَّىٰهَا” (91:3), which reveals the sun; the named object makes the earlier, more directed unveiling concrete.
The source section names root غ ش و for night covering; 91:4 gives that same covering verb an object, the sun, clarifying what 92:1 leaves unstated.
The section's objectless night spreads over what is visible; “يُغْشِي ٱلَّيْلَ ٱلنَّهَارَ” depicts God covering day with night and adds their rapid pursuit and created order.

This verse says God makes night cover day (“يُغْشِي ٱلَّيْلَ ٱلنَّهَارَ”) amid the earth's rivers; the source section's root notes connect النهار both to daylight and, in a secondary dictionary form, a river that splits earth.

The verse calls night and day two signs, then says the night sign is erased and the day sign made visible (“مُبْصِرَةً”); this makes explicit the revelation and concealment that the section reads in their paired actions.
The section has night laying a cover and day opening into view; this reverses the covering image by stripping (“نَسْلَخُ”) day out of night, producing the same transition from dark to visible.
The verse says God wraps night over day and day over night (“يُكَوِّرُ”); this is another concrete model of the two layers rolling across one another.
Where the section gives day the act of appearing, this verse says God darkened the night and brought out its brightness (“أَخْرَجَ ضُحَىٰهَا”), making the emergence from darkness explicit.

The section names root ج ل و for disclosure and says its force can exceed what the veiled scene can bear; here “تَجَلَّىٰ رَبُّهُۥ لِلْجَبَلِ” and the mountain's collapse give that unveiling a perilous boundary.
The source section names dictionary form غِشَاوَة as a covering over eyes; this verse places “غِشَاوَةٌ” over rejecters' sight, so the covering becomes a failure to receive what is disclosed.

The source section connects غ ش و with a veil over sight; this verse says a person who makes desire his god has “غِشَاوَةً” over his sight, then asks who can guide him, joining veil to the guidance the section attributes to God.
The section warns against remaining covered when daylight opens; “فَأَغْشَيْنَٰهُمْ فَهُمْ لَا يُبْصِرُونَ” shows a covering that directly prevents seeing.
This verse reverses the world's cover: God removes the person's covering (“كَشَفْنَا عَنكَ غِطَآءَكَ”) and sight is keen that day, directly completing the section's concealment-and-disclosure pair.
The source section extends غ ش و to a sensory barrier; Noah says his people “ٱسْتَغْشَوْا۟ ثِيَابَهُمْ” when called, using covering to enact refusal to hear guidance even as it is brought to them.

The section's dictionary gloss relates a covering over the heart to the rust of habit; this verse calls people's deeds a “رَانَ” over their hearts, a precise Qur'anic counterpart for that secondary heart-covering sense.

After 83:14's rust on hearts, this verse says wrongdoers will be screened from their Lord (“لَمَحْجُوبُونَ”); its contribution is the final barrier that makes inner veiling an encounter with withheld vision.
The source section gives al-ghāshiya as an event that envelops creation; this verse asks whether people feel secure from “غَٰشِيَةٌ” of God's punishment arriving suddenly while they are unaware.
This verse says punishment will cover people (“يَغْشَىٰهُمُ ٱلْعَذَابُ”) from above and beneath; it gives the source section's all-enveloping غ ش و image a bodily, inescapable form.
The section identifies al-ghāshiya as the Resurrection that covers creation with terror; the same named event opens this surah in “حَدِيثُ ٱلْغَٰشِيَةِ.”
The section describes wrongdoing as faces covered by night; this verse says faces are as if covered with dark pieces of night (“أُغْشِيَتْ وُجُوهُهُمْ”), making the concealment an outcome of evil.
The verse uses the same covering root named by the section: “وَتَغْشَىٰ وُجُوهَهُمُ ٱلنَّارُ,” with fire covering faces.
Against the section's image of faces darkened or covered, this verse says no grime or humiliation overwhelms the faces of those who do good; it marks a contrary face-outcome.
The section says covering is not inherently harmful; after Uhud, secure drowsiness “يَغْشَىٰ طَآئِفَةًۭ” of believers, a protective, restful use of the same root.
The verse pairs the splitting of dawn (“فَالِقُ ٱلْإِصْبَاحِ”) with night made for rest; it stages the opening edge of day beside the night's covering and rest.
“جَعَلَ لَكُمُ ٱلَّيْلَ لِبَاسًا” calls night a garment, then pairs sleep as rest with day as dispersal; it directly develops covering as a beneficial night/day cycle.
The source section says night is also a sign that gives rest; this neighboring verse identifies sleep as repose, the human counterpart to the nighttime covering in 78:10.
“جَعَلْنَا ٱلَّيْلَ لِبَاسًا” gives night the very covering image developed in the section, now as a garment over human activity.
After 78:10's night-as-garment, this verse makes day a time of livelihood; its own contribution is the exposed, active counterpart that completes the pair.
The verse explicitly makes night for rest and day “مُبْصِرًا” (giving sight); this directly joins the section's night-covering and daylight-disclosure to their human effects.
The verse asks whether people see that night was made for rest and day “مُبْصِرًا”; the daylight-as-sight wording directly echoes the section's image of what the opened day makes visible.
This verse again says night is for rest and day for sight (“مُبْصِرًا”), treating the pair as divine favor; its repeated formulation confirms the section's positive night/day function.
The verse asks who could bring light (“بِضِيَاءٍ”) if God made night last until Resurrection; it reverses the ordinary day that breaks the covering and exposes the world.
Following 28:71's unending night, this verse asks who could bring night for rest if day lasted forever; it supplies the opposite boundary, showing each phase by what the other provides.
After the two impossible extremes in 28:71–72, this verse says mercy gave people night and day for rest and seeking bounty; it names the balance the section's paired operations imply.

The verse says God makes night enter day and day enter night (“تُولِجُ ٱلَّيْلَ فِى ٱلنَّهَارِ”); its interpenetrating cycle complements the section's image of one layer covering and the other opening.
This verse repeats God's causing night to enter day and day to enter night, adding that He is Hearing and Seeing; the seeing language makes the cycle legible as divine sign and order.
“يُقَلِّبُ ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّيْلَ وَٱلنَّهَارَ” names God's turning of the two phases and calls it a lesson for those with sight, connecting the section's visible alternation to perception.
The verse says God makes night enter day and day enter night and subjects sun and moon to their terms; it adds the measured cosmic order behind the section's recurring disclosure.

This verse says God makes night enter day and day enter night, then denies that those invoked besides Him own even a membrane; the created alternation sets a boundary between God and powerless rivals.
The verse repeats the night/day interpenetration and adds that God knows what breasts conceal; this links the seen alternation to the hidden interior that the section's covering image evokes.
The verse says the sun and moon are made constant in their courses and night and day are made subject to human use; it situates the section's two processes within ordered provision.
The verse names night and day alongside sun and moon and says each swims in an orbit; it adds that their alternation belongs to a governed cosmic order, not an isolated visual effect.
The verse pairs life and death with the alternation of night and day; this places the visible cycle the section describes alongside the passage of created life.
This verse calls night, day, sun, and moon among God's signs and forbids worship of the luminaries; it makes the section's visible pair signs pointing beyond themselves.
The alternation of night and day is called a sign for people of understanding; this states the perceptual and reflective force of the pair on which the section dwells.
This verse lists the alternation of night and day among God's signs for people who reason, affirming that the paired scene itself invites reflection.
The verse swears by night as it departs (“إِذْ أَدْبَرَ”); it gives the night-covering image its reverse motion, withdrawal.
After 74:33's departing night, this verse swears by morning as it brightens (“إِذَا أَسْفَرَ”); it supplies the visible counterpart that completes the scene.
Following the departing night and brightening morning in 74:33–34, this verse calls the scene one of the great signs; its own contribution is to mark their alternation as weighty evidence.
The verse swears by night when it recedes or gathers (“عَسْعَسَ,” whose direction is uncertain); either reading places night at a changing boundary, as in the section's passing cover.
After 81:17's turning night, this verse swears by morning as it breathes (“تَنَفَّسَ”); its own contribution is the image of day opening into life.
This verse swears by twilight (“بِٱلشَّفَقِ”), the visible threshold as day gives way; it extends the section's concern with changing visibility at nightfall.
After 84:16's twilight, “وَٱلَّيْلِ وَمَا وَسَقَ” evokes night and what it gathers; it makes night an enveloping collection rather than a bare time-name.
The dawn oath (“وَٱلْفَجْرِ”) isolates the moment when the section's hidden world begins to become visible.
The verse swears by night as it passes (“إِذَا يَسْرِ”), another direct image of the covering phase withdrawing before day.

In the parable, a fire lights the surroundings and then God takes away their light, leaving them in darkness unable to see; this makes illumination's disappearance a specific image of covered perception.
The storm parable says lightning nearly snatches their sight and that they walk when it lights for them but stop in darkness; it dramatizes the unstable boundary between visibility and concealment.

Moses sees a fire and hopes to bring a brand or find guidance there; the source section labels the root family of نار with a dictionary form for lamp-wick soot used as eye pigment, and this scene gives fire a concrete illuminating and guiding role.
Moses sees a fire and hopes for news or a burning brand; as in the section's secondary dictionary link between نار and light used at the eye, the fire is a possible source of illumination.
Moses sees a fire and hopes for news or a brand to warm his family; this repeated fire scene gives the section's secondary fire/light association a practical, human use.

The source section names a dictionary form from the root family of نار/نور as lamp-wick soot used for kohl; this verse's niche, lamp, and shining light offer a Qur'anic lamp image that makes the fire/light/sight association concrete.

The source section says huda has the dictionary sense bayān, clarification, and assigns disclosure to God; this verse says revelation brings people from darkness into light by their Lord's permission.

God brings believers from darkness into light, while false patrons bring disbelievers from light into darkness; this reversal makes the section's unveiling and its warning about refusing to see morally consequential.
The source section explicitly labels the dictionary sense of هدى as البيان; this verse places “بَيَانٌ” beside “هُدًۭى,” directly supporting that lexical link and tying guidance to clarification.

The section says the day makes separate human courses visible; this verse says God will distinguish the corrupt from the good (“يَمِيزَ ٱلْخَبِيثَ مِنَ ٱلطَّيِّبِ”), naming that disclosure of difference.
The verse says testing makes evident those who are truthful and those who lie; it parallels the section's image of a later opening that exposes courses hidden beneath a common cover.
“يَوْمَ تُبْلَى ٱلسَّرَآئِرُ” says hidden inward matters are tested and exposed; it gives the section's concealment/disclosure image an inward, final-day counterpart.

On the final day, hypocrites ask for believers' light and a wall is placed between them; the partition and separate light make the section's claim that apparently shared space conceals divergent courses concrete.
This verse describes faces turning white or black on the Day; visible faces disclose a difference that the section's day-opening image presents as hidden until it appears.
“وُجُوهٌۭ يَوْمَئِذٍۢ نَّاضِرَةٌ” shows radiant faces on that Day; the source section sets the word-family of 92:20's sought “face” beside the dictionary phrase “face of day” for its first opening.

After 75:22's radiant faces, this verse says they look toward their Lord (“إِلَىٰ رَبِّهَا نَاظِرَةٌ”); it connects the source section's face-word link to the act of seeing that its disclosure image foregrounds.
This verse says faces on that Day bear dust (“غَبَرَةٌ”); the visible mark contrasts with the unclouded disclosure in the section and prepares the explicit dark covering in 80:41.
After 80:40's dust-covered faces, this verse says darkness covers them (“تَرْهَقُهَا قَتَرَةٌ”); it closely matches the section's image of night-darkness covering faces.
The verse says those who lied about God will have blackened faces on the Day; as with the section's covered faces, inner refusal becomes an outwardly visible state.

The source section's secondary dictionary account says a river splits the earth; here earth's springs burst open (“وَفَجَّرْنَا ٱلْأَرْضَ عُيُونًا”), a related but not identical image of the ground opening to release what was within.
